| [LIT-714](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-714.md) v2 | The Method of Characteristics Revisited: A Viability Approach | Aubin (1999), lecture notes on arXiv. A set K is viable under a system if from each state in K at least one evolution stays in K, and invariant if every evolution does. By Nagumo's theorem K is viable exactly when the dynamics point into K's contingent cone at each state. The viability kernel of K is the largest viable subset of K; its complement in K is a repeller. The capture basin of a target is the set of states from which it can be reached in finite time. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-576](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-576.md)): the introduction and chapters 1–2 of the author's arXiv lecture notes, the parts that define viability. Worth reading as the shortest first-hand statement the record holds of Aubin's viability concepts: a set is viable if from every state at least one evolution stays in it, invariant if all do, and the viability kernel is the largest viable subset of a constraint set. Chapters 3 onward apply these to Hamilton–Jacobi equations and were not read. Stands in for the unread monograph [LIT-738](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-738.md). |

| [LIT-1292](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1292.md) v3 | A contraction based, singular perturbation approach to near-decomposability in complex systems | Bousquet & Slotine (arXiv 2015, unpublished). Recasts Simon's near-decomposability as a singularly perturbed system, fast module states x̃ and slow states y with ẏ = O(ε), and bounds the error of the reduced slow system with nonlinear contraction theory. If each module is contracting, the reduced slow system is contracting, and the coupling terms grow at most affinely in \|x̃\| and \|y\|, then below an explicit critical separation ε_c, after a transient of order (1/β_f + 1/(εβ_g)) log(1/ε), the fast states stay O(ε) from their quasi-steady values and the slow states O(ε) from the reduced trajectory, for all later time. A worked building example with a negative conductance shows multiple equilibria and instability above ε_c. Read it knowing that it is a five-page preprint, never published in a journal, whose proofs are sketches; that Remark 8 prints ε_c inverted (the worked example's value √2/7 is the reciprocal of the printed expression, and matches Hypothesis 2); that Lemma 3's O(ε) bound on the slow error needs d_g = 0, which the proof's last line assumes silently while the worked example lists d_g = 1; that it is deterministic throughout and bounds trajectory error only, not any information-theoretic dependence; that the slow coordinates and the partition are given, not found; and that ε_c is sufficient and in linear checks conservative by factors of 3 to 50. |
| [LIT-1880](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1880.md) v2 | When Can Safe Controllers Adapt? Information before Commitment | Saligrama (2026). A safe adaptive controller must stay safe under every model not yet ruled out. Its first action that leaves no safe continuation under an alternative is a commitment, and the observation that action produces comes too late to justify it. With the information before commitment measured as a KL divergence between stopped records, every uniformly safe policy forfeits at least about ½e^{−I} of the value reachable only by committing. Acting on an exclusion at risk α needs about log(1/(2α)) nats beforehand. Bounded information and a linear gap give linear regret, shown for a headroom-limited device and for constrained linear regulation. Finite information can still certify a smaller candidate list. Safe recovery at O(√(T log T)) holds when a safe experiment is repeatable, informative and returns to a common state. | Active — read in full 2026-10-31 ([NOTE-1466](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1466.md)), with the main proofs; worth reading for the precise sense in which evidence must precede commitment: the observation a committing action produces cannot justify it, and bounded information before commitment leaves a fixed fraction of the oracle gap to every uniformly safe controller ([THEORY-1254](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1254.md)). It also proves the positive case, safe recovery from a repeatable informative experiment, and shows certainty equivalence failing at an active constraint ([THEORY-1256](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1256.md)). |
| [LIT-1893](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1893.md) v2 | Input-to-State Safety With Control Barrier Functions | Kolathaya & Ames (2019). Defines input-to-state safety for a safe set C = {h ≥ 0}: under an input disturbance bounded by ‖d‖∞, the larger set {h + γ(‖d‖∞) ≥ 0} stays forward invariant, for some class-K γ. A barrier inequality with a disturbance penalty, ḣ ≥ −α(h) − ι(‖d‖), implies it. Adding a damping term εL_g hᵀ to any barrier controller, or the matching constraint to a CLF–CBF quadratic program, gives ι = ‖d‖²/(4ε). The paper's examples show that nominal barrier controllers, including the standard quadratic program, can leave the safe set without bound under small disturbances. | Active — read in full 2026-10-31 ([NOTE-1477](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1477.md)); worth reading as the short statement of graded robust safety: under a bounded input disturbance a barrier-function controller keeps the state not in the safe set but in a set enlarged by a class-K function of the disturbance, and a damping term along the barrier's input direction delivers this with an enlargement of ‖d‖²/(4ε) ([THEORY-1267](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1267.md)). It is not the robust box invariance [CASE-190](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-190.md) certifies, which is [THEORY-134](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-134.md)'s. |

| [LIT-2020](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2020.md) | Nonholonomic motion planning: steering using sinusoids | Murray & Sastry (1993). Robots whose velocity constraints do not integrate to constraints on configuration (a car, a car with trailers, a hopping robot in flight, fingers rolling on an object) are written as driftless control systems whose input vector fields span the directions the system can move in. By Chow's theorem the system is controllable when those fields and their iterated Lie brackets span every direction; a bracket is the net motion left by a small loop of inputs. The paper steers first the directly actuated states and then each bracket direction in turn with sinusoids at integrally related frequencies, shows that this fails for general higher-order systems, and defines chained systems, for which it works, with a sufficient condition for converting a two-input system to chained form by feedback. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1622](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1622.md)) from the scanned IEEE PDF in CaltechAUTHORS, the first author's institutional repository; worth reading as the standard constructive account of steering nonholonomic systems, for how it rewrites velocity constraints as the directions a system can move in, recovers the forbidden directions as Lie brackets reached only by cycling the inputs, and steers chained systems with sinusoids at integrally related frequencies. Its main limits: the results are local, for driftless, regular systems in free space; the conversion to chained form is only sufficient; simple sinusoids fail for general higher-order systems; closed-loop control and systems with drift are left open. |

| [LIT-2050](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2050.md) | Stability principle underlying passive dynamic walking of rimless wheel | Asano (2012). A rimless wheel rolling down a slope loses a fixed fraction of its kinetic energy at each impact, ε = cos²α for leg angle α, and regains a fixed amount from gravity each step, so the step-to-step energy converges to a single value: the gait is asymptotically stable and period-1. A linearised stance phase gives the return map's eigenvalue as cos²α, fixed by the wheel's geometry and independent of the step period, a closed form for the step period, and a minimum slope, tan²(α/2) in the linearised model, below which the wheel cannot pass over mid-stance. On steep slopes walking turns to running or skipping. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1578](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1578.md)) from the author's arXiv deposit of the 2012 conference paper; worth reading as a short analytic account of why the passive rimless wheel's gravity-powered gait is stable: the impact posture and the energy restored each step are fixed by geometry, so the return map's eigenvalue is cos²α whatever the step period, and the gait exists only above a minimum slope. Registered as a neighbour standing in for McGeer (1990), [LIT-2108](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2108.md), on the rimless wheel only. Its main limits: a linearised, planar, one-degree-of-freedom model, so the result does not by itself extend to walkers with a swing leg, and the upper slope limit is not identified. |
| [LIT-2056](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2056.md) v2 | Planning and acting in partially observable stochastic domains | Kaelbling, Littman & Cassandra (1998). An agent that cannot observe the state keeps a belief state, a probability distribution over states updated by Bayes' rule, which is a sufficient statistic for its history; control then becomes an MDP over beliefs. The optimal t-step value is the upper surface of one linear function per policy tree, so it is piecewise-linear and convex, and the optimal policy partitions belief space into polyhedral regions. The paper adds the witness algorithm and the tiger problem, where with two steps to go the optimal policy only listens. It credits Smallwood and Sondik with the belief state's sufficiency (jointly with another work) and an exact direct-construction algorithm that is exponential in the worst case. | Active — read 2026-11-04 and 2026-11-06 (NOTE-1563, Read for the parts on the belief state and the value function) from the published PDF on the first author's MIT CSAIL page; worth reading as the standard restatement, for an AI readership, of the operations-research theory of partially observable Markov decision processes: the belief state as a sufficient statistic, control as an MDP over beliefs, the piecewise-linear convex finite-horizon value function, and the tiger problem, in which a costly, noisy information action is valued inside the model. Registered as the stand-in for Smallwood and Sondik (1973), [LIT-2038](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2038.md), whose core finite-horizon results it restates. Its main limits: enumerated rather than factored states, a known model, and exact solution intractable in general. |
| [LIT-2077](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2077.md) | Approximating complex 3D curves using origami spring structures | Liu, Zhang & Fang (2023). An origami spring, two perpendicular paper strips folded alternately, is not rigid-foldable, because its square facets bend. A virtual crease along each facet's diagonal makes each cell a one-degree-of-freedom unit, and the chain of cells is fitted to a target 3D curve by optimising the folding angles. With one angle per cell the relative error was below 0.66% for C, J and spiral curves. Grouping cells to share actuators, two sufficed for the C and spiral curves and three for the J; a sinusoidal curve needed more, and each added actuator reduced the error by less. Prototypes driven by cables and servos reproduced the C, J and spiral shapes, with errors near the drive end from gravity and friction. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1558](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1558.md)) from the publisher's open-access PDF (CC BY 4.0); worth reading as a worked case of underactuation as a design choice: an origami spring, made rigid-foldable by virtual creases, is fitted to 3D curves with its cells grouped to share a few actuators, and the fitting error falls with each added actuator, by less each time. Its main limits: a kinematic model with no stiffness, gravity or friction, a virtual-crease approximation asserted rather than quantified, a penalty heuristic with no optimality guarantee, and prototypes for three curves only. |

| [LIT-2110](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2110.md) | Formation mechanism of a basin of attraction for passive dynamic walking induced by intrinsic hyperbolicity | Obayashi, Aoi, Tsuchiya & Kokubu (2016). In Garcia et al.'s simplest walking model, two massless legs with point masses on a slope and no control, the set of initial states that take at least one step, pulled back through the step map, gives nested sets whose intersection is the basin of attraction of the gait. The basin is very small, thin and V-shaped, with fractal-like slits and stripes. The authors trace this to the upright equilibrium, a saddle-centre: the stance leg behaves as an inverted pendulum, and regions pulled back near the saddle's stable manifold are thinned and folded. As the slope grows, the attractor goes through period doubling to chaos and then meets the basin boundary and disappears. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1586](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1586.md)) from the authors' arXiv version (CC BY 4.0); worth reading as a dynamical-systems explanation of why passive walkers are hard to make walk: the basin of attraction of the simplest walking model is small, thin and fractal-like because its upright equilibrium is a saddle, and as the slope grows the gait goes through period doubling to chaos and is destroyed by a boundary crisis. Registered as a neighbour standing in for McGeer (1990), [LIT-2108](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2108.md), on the idea of passive dynamic walking and the later findings on its stability. Its main limits: one idealised model in a singular limit, basin membership by finite-step numerics, and a mechanism argued from a linearisation and figures rather than proved. |
